Description: This term names a single consonant sound that starts with a complete closure of the vocal tract, exactly like an ordinary stop, but then releases that closure gradually into a narrow gap rather than opening freely, so that a short burst of frication noise follows the closure at the same place of articulation. Because the closure and the following frication occur together at one location and are treated by speakers as a single phonological unit rather than two separate sounds, this sound patterns as one segment in syllable structure and in phonological rules, and it is counted as only one sound when speakers judge how many sounds a word contains. English has two such sounds, both produced at the post-alveolar region, one voiceless and one voiced. These sounds are common across languages but not universal, and languages differ in how many such combinations of closure-plus-frication they contrast. In feature terms, this sound is usually described as having a delayed release compared with a plain stop, capturing the brief but audible frication that follows the closure before the articulators separate fully.
Example: The 'ch' in 'church' /tʃɜːrtʃ/ and the 'j' in 'judge' /dʒʌdʒ/ each combine a stop-like closure with a following burst of frication at the same place of articulation.

Description: This term refers to one of the different phonetic realizations that a single phoneme can take on the surface, that is, one of the variant pronunciations a speaker produces without that variation changing the identity or meaning of the word. Such variants typically arise from predictable phonetic context, such as the position of a sound within the syllable or word, the sounds surrounding it, or the presence of stress nearby, and their distribution is described by phonological rules that state exactly where each variant occurs. Crucially, substituting one variant for another in this relationship never creates a new word or a different meaning; native speakers usually are not consciously aware of the difference unless it is pointed out, since the variants are treated mentally as the same underlying sound. This relationship contrasts with contrastive sound units capable of distinguishing meaning on their own. The link between an underlying sound category and its surface variants is central to phonological analysis, since much of phonology is devoted to discovering which phonetic differences are predictable and non-contrastive in this way and which instead distinguish meaning in a given language.
Example: In English, the puff of air heard in [pʰ] in 'pin' and its absence in [p] in 'spin' are two surface variants of one and the same underlying /p/.

Description: This term describes a situation in which a single morpheme is pronounced differently depending on the phonological or morphological environment it appears in, so that the same underlying unit surfaces as two or more distinct forms. Such patterns can be purely phonological, triggered automatically by nearby sounds or stress and predictable by a general rule, or they can be conditioned morphologically, occurring only in specific grammatical contexts such as particular suffixes or irregular paradigms. Identifying this kind of variation is one of the main tasks of phonological analysis, because the pattern often reveals what the underlying representation of a morpheme is and what rules apply to derive the different surface forms. Linguists distinguish cases that are still phonologically active and productive from those that have become lexicalized historical relics no longer governed by any live rule in the synchronic grammar. Studying such patterns helps explain why related words in the same language family can sound quite different on the surface while still being recognized by speakers as forms built on the same root.
Example: The regular plural suffix surfaces as [s], [z], or [ɪz] depending on context, as in 'cats' [kæts], 'dogs' [dɒgz], and 'buses' [bʌsɪz].

Description: This term names a place of articulation in which the active articulator, usually the tip or blade of the tongue, makes contact with or approaches the bony ridge located just behind the upper front teeth. This place of articulation is extremely common across the world's languages and typically supports several different manners of articulation, since a wide range of consonant types, including stops, fricatives, nasals, laterals, and approximants, can all be produced comfortably at this location. In English specifically, this region hosts one of the richest sets of contrasting consonants in the entire inventory, more than any other single place of articulation, reflecting how flexible and precisely controllable the tongue tip is for making fine articulatory distinctions. Consonants made here are often contrasted with sounds made at neighboring places, such as those made at or near the teeth and those made slightly further back, and learners of English as a second language sometimes need to adjust the precise tongue placement if their native language uses a nearby but distinct place of articulation.
Example: /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/, /n/, and /l/ in English are all made at this same place of articulation, as in 'tap', 'dip', 'sun', 'zoo', 'nap', and 'lip'.

Description: This term names the phenomenon in which a single consonant appears to belong simultaneously to two adjacent syllables rather than being clearly assigned to only the end of the first syllable or only the beginning of the second. This typically occurs with an intervocalic consonant following a short, stressed vowel, where phonetic evidence, such as the degree of aspiration, vowel length, or resyllabification behavior in fast speech, suggests that the consonant is shared between the preceding and following syllables rather than uniquely owned by either one. Positing such double membership is proposed as a solution to cases where straightforward syllabification rules give conflicting or ambiguous results, and it has consequences for stress assignment, for judgments about syllable weight, and for rules that are sensitive to whether a consonant counts as closing one syllable or opening the next. Not all phonologists accept this device as theoretically necessary, and some frameworks instead handle the same facts through resyllabification rules or gradient phonetic detail, but the notion remains a useful way of describing the intuitive 'in-between' status that certain medial consonants seem to have.
Example: The /p/ in 'happy' is often analyzed as belonging to both syllables at once, as if the word were split either hap.py or ha.ppy.

Description: This term names a burst of voiceless airflow that follows the release of certain voiceless stop consonants before the onset of voicing for a following vowel or sonorant, measured phonetically as a delay, called voice onset time, between the release of the closure and the start of vocal fold vibration. In English, this property is not contrastive on its own but is instead automatic and rule-governed: voiceless stops carry it in certain strong positions, such as at the beginning of a stressed syllable, and lack it in weaker positions, such as after /s/ or in unstressed syllables, making the two variants allophones of the same phoneme rather than separate sounds. In many other languages, however, this same property is phonemic, meaning that stops with and without it contrast directly and can distinguish otherwise identical words, so learners whose native language does not use it contrastively must learn to both perceive and control it consciously. It is typically transcribed with a small raised h, and its presence or absence is one of the clearest acoustic cues that phoneticians use to classify stop consonants across languages.
Example: The /p/ in 'pin' [pʰɪn] carries this puff of breath, while the /p/ in 'spin' [spɪn] lacks it, though both represent the same phoneme /p/.

Description: One of this pair of opposite processes occurs when one sound becomes more similar to, or identical with, a neighboring sound, typically by taking on one or more of its phonetic features such as place of articulation, manner, voicing, or nasality; this is extremely common across languages because it reflects the physiological tendency of articulators to move efficiently and anticipate or carry over gestures from adjacent sounds, and it can apply within a word, across morpheme boundaries, or even across word boundaries in connected speech. The other, much rarer process is the opposite: two sounds that are similar or identical become less alike, usually to make them easier to perceive as distinct or easier to articulate in sequence. Both processes can be regressive, where a sound is influenced by a following sound, or progressive, where a sound is influenced by a preceding one, and both are frequently invoked to explain historical sound changes as well as synchronic alternations that speakers apply automatically in everyday speech.
Example: The prefix 'in-' takes on the place of articulation of a following /p/, /b/, or /m/, giving 'impossible' rather than 'inpossible'.

Description: This first term names a place of articulation in which the two lips come together to form a complete or partial closure of the vocal tract, one of the most basic and cross-linguistically common places of articulation because it requires no precise tongue positioning. The broader category to which it belongs covers any sound involving the lips as an active articulator, which also includes sounds in which the lower lip approaches the upper teeth, and sounds in which lip rounding combines simultaneously with a raising of the back of the tongue toward the velum, the latter being doubly articulated because they have two simultaneous primary constrictions of roughly equal importance rather than one primary and one secondary articulation. These related but distinct categories are important to keep separate because they behave differently in phonological rules and can pattern with different natural classes depending on the language, even though all of them share the common feature of active lip involvement.
Example: /p, b, m/ involve only the two lips, as in 'pat', 'bat', and 'mat', unlike /f, v/, which involve the lower lip against the upper teeth, or /w/, which adds lip rounding to tongue-back raising.

Description: This pair of variant pronunciations of the lateral approximant phoneme /l/ differ mainly in the position and shape of the tongue body, particularly whether the back of the tongue is raised toward the velum. One variant is produced with a relatively flat tongue body and little or no velar raising, giving it a brighter, more front-vowel-like acoustic quality, whereas the other, often called the velarized variant, involves simultaneous raising of the back of the tongue toward the soft palate, giving it a lower, more back-vowel-like resonance. In many varieties of English, the distribution of these two variants is governed by syllable position: the brighter variant tends to occur in syllable-initial position, especially before a vowel, while the velarized variant tends to occur in syllable-final position or before a consonant. Because this distribution is predictable from context and does not create meaning contrasts, the two variants are treated as allophones of a single phoneme rather than as separate phonemes, even though listeners can often hear the acoustic difference once it is pointed out.
Example: In many English accents, the 'l' in 'leaf' [liːf] has a brighter quality, while the 'l' in 'feel' [fiːɫ] has a lower, velarized quality.

Description: One member of this pair of syllable types ends in one or more consonants, meaning it has a filled position following the vowel nucleus, whereas the other member ends in a vowel with nothing filling that following position at all, so that the vowel itself is the final sound of the syllable. This distinction matters for several areas of phonology, including vowel length and quality, since many languages show systematic differences in how vowels are realized depending on which of the two syllable types they occur in, and it also matters for syllable weight, because the consonant-final type is often, though not universally, treated as heavier than the vowel-final type for purposes of stress assignment. In English spelling instruction, this pair of syllable types is frequently used pedagogically to help learners predict vowel pronunciation, since a vowel followed by nothing is often long or tense while the same letter followed by a consonant is often short or lax, although this correspondence is only a rough tendency rather than an exceptionless rule.
Example: 'Go' [goʊ] ends directly in a vowel, while 'got' [gɒt] ends in the consonant /t/ following the same vowel quality.

Description: This term names the portion of a syllable that follows the vowel nucleus, consisting of one or more consonants that close off the syllable, and together with the onset and nucleus it forms the basic tripartite structure that phonologists use to describe syllable-internal organization. Not every syllable has this constituent; syllables without one are called open, while those with one are called closed, and languages vary enormously in how many consonants they permit in this position, ranging from none at all to complex consonant clusters. This constituent is important for determining syllable weight, since a syllable that has one is often treated as heavier than an open syllable with the same vowel, which in turn can influence stress placement and other prosodic patterns. Consonants in this position are also frequently subject to special phonological processes not found at the beginning of a syllable, such as neutralization of certain contrasts, devoicing, or lack of release, because articulatory and perceptual pressures often differ between the beginning and the end of a syllable.
Example: In the word 'cats' [kæts], the consonant cluster /ts/ following the vowel /æ/ closes off the syllable.

Description: This term describes the relationship between two or more sounds when each occurs only in a specific, mutually exclusive set of phonetic environments, such that the sounds never appear in the same context and their occurrence can be fully predicted from the surrounding environment. This pattern is one of the primary types of evidence phonologists use to argue that two phonetically different sounds are variants of a single underlying phoneme rather than separate phonemes, because if the difference between the sounds is entirely predictable from context, speakers do not need to store both as distinct contrastive units; the variation can instead be generated by a general rule. This relationship is usually established by examining minimal pairs and environments systematically, and it is often accompanied by phonetic similarity between the sounds in question, since variants of the same phoneme also tend to share articulatory or acoustic properties even as their exact distribution differs. This pattern stands in contrast to a relationship in which two sounds occur in the same environment and create a meaning difference, marking them as separate phonemes.
Example: Aspirated [pʰ] occurs only syllable-initially and unaspirated [p] occurs only after /s/ or in codas, so the two never occur in the same environment.

Description: This term names a phonological rule that applies automatically as the general, unmarked case unless some more specific rule or condition intervenes to block or override it, effectively supplying a predictable value or realization whenever no special conditioning environment is present. Such a rule is often described as applying elsewhere, meaning it covers whatever contexts are left over once all more narrowly conditioned rules have been accounted for, which is why it is closely associated with the elsewhere condition in rule-based phonology. Because it represents the least marked or most general outcome, it is typically ordered to apply after more specific rules, ensuring that those narrower rules get the first opportunity to apply in their limited environments before the broader, general statement fills in the rest of the cases. This organizational principle helps linguists write economical grammars, since instead of listing every possible context individually, they can state one specific rule for exceptional environments and let a single general statement automatically handle every other environment.
Example: If a language voices stops between vowels but otherwise keeps stops voiceless everywhere else, the voicing statement is specific and the voicelessness is the general fallback.

Description: This term names a place of articulation in which the tip or blade of the tongue makes contact with or approaches the upper front teeth, distinguishing it from a place slightly further back at the bony ridge behind the teeth, and from a place in which the tongue protrudes between the upper and lower teeth. Sounds made here are found in many of the world's languages, sometimes contrasting directly with sounds made at the neighboring ridge in the same language, which requires speakers to control fine differences in tongue-tip placement that can be difficult for second-language learners whose native language does not make this same distinction. In English, true sounds of this type exist and are sometimes described more precisely with an additional label because the tongue tip is visible between the teeth during their production, while other consonants sometimes loosely associated with this region are more accurately classified as belonging to the ridge just behind the teeth. Cross-linguistically, this contrast with the neighboring place is one of the more perceptually subtle place-of-articulation distinctions, and phonetic transcription systems provide dedicated symbols and diacritics specifically to keep the two clearly distinguished in careful analysis.
Example: The English fricatives /θ/ and /ð/, as in 'thin' and 'this', are produced with the tongue tip at or between the upper front teeth.

Description: In phonology, this term refers to the step-by-step sequence of rule applications that maps an abstract underlying representation of a word onto its concrete surface pronunciation, with each rule in the sequence potentially changing, adding, or deleting features, segments, or structure based on the output of the previous step. Classical generative phonology models pronunciation as the output of ordered rules operating on an underlying form, so this sequence is essentially a formal proof showing exactly how and why a particular surface form arises from its underlying representation, including which rules apply, in what order, and what the intermediate representations look like at each stage. The order in which rules apply within this sequence can crucially affect the final output, since applying two rules in one order may produce a different surface form than applying the same two rules in the opposite order, which is why rule ordering is a central topic connected closely to this concept. Making this sequence explicit is also used pedagogically to state clear, testable claims about the phonological system of a language, since a well-formed sequence of this kind should correctly predict the attested surface forms for a given set of inputs.
Example: A step-by-step account might show /ɪn+pasəbl/ undergoing nasal place assimilation to surface as [ɪmpasəbl] 'impossible', with each intermediate step made explicit.

Description: This process occurs when a segment that is normally or underlyingly voiced loses its voicing and is realized instead as a voiceless, or at least partially voiceless, sound, typically because of its position in the word, its proximity to other voiceless sounds, or general prosodic weakening at edges of words or utterances. It is extremely common cross-linguistically in final position, where obstruents at the end of a word or syllable frequently lose contrastive voicing even if the same sound is reliably voiced elsewhere in the language. This process can be a completely automatic, allophonic phonetic process that applies without exception in a given environment, or it can be a more variable, gradient phenomenon whose degree depends on speech rate, style, and individual speaker tendencies, and phoneticians distinguish a partial version, in which some voicing remains but is reduced, from a complete version, in which voicing is entirely absent. This process is important both for describing individual languages and for understanding broader patterns of markedness, since voiceless obstruents are generally considered less marked than their voiced counterparts.
Example: In German, word-final /d/ loses its voicing and surfaces as [t], so 'Rad' (wheel) is pronounced [ʁaːt] despite being spelled with 'd'.

Description: One member of this pair of perspectives refers to the study of language as it changes over historical time, tracing how sounds, forms, or structures evolve from one stage of a language to a later stage, whereas the other member refers to the study of a language system as it exists at a single point in time, without reference to its history or later development. A shift viewed from the first perspective, then, is any historical alteration in pronunciation, such as a sound merging with another sound, splitting into two distinct sounds, or shifting its place or manner of articulation, that can be documented by comparing earlier and later stages of a language or by comparing related languages that descended from a common ancestor. The second perspective, by contrast, focuses purely on the internal logic and rule system operating in a language at one moment, treating that system as a self-contained object of study regardless of how it came to be that way historically. The distinction between these two perspectives, originally emphasized by Ferdinand de Saussure, remains foundational in linguistics because a pattern that looks arbitrary or irregular from the second viewpoint often becomes fully explainable once its history is understood.
Example: The Great Vowel Shift is a well-known historical change tracked across centuries, while a description of present-day English vowel contrasts looks only at one moment in time.

Description: One member of this pair of vowel types involves a perceptible change in quality within a single syllable, as the tongue and lips glide smoothly from one vowel target toward another target without any intervening consonant, so that the whole sequence is treated phonologically as one vowel nucleus rather than as two separate vowels in two syllables. The other member, by contrast, has a single, relatively steady articulatory target throughout its duration, without this kind of internal glide in quality. The gliding type is often transcribed with two vowel symbols joined together to represent the starting and ending points of the movement, and languages differ both in how many such vowels they have and in how phonologists analyze their internal structure, with some frameworks treating the second element as behaving more like a glide consonant than a true vowel. Distinguishing a gliding vowel from a sequence of a vowel plus a following glide consonant, or from two vowels in separate syllables, can be an important and sometimes subtle analytical decision, since the phonetic signal alone does not always make the syllabification unambiguous.
Example: The vowel in 'boy' [bɔɪ] glides from one quality to another within a single syllable, while the vowel in 'bee' [biː] holds a single steady quality throughout.

Terminology: dual articulation (or secondary articulation: e.g., lip rounding in /ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/)
Description: This term refers to a situation in which a consonant has one primary constriction that defines its basic place and manner of articulation along with an additional, simultaneous articulatory gesture layered on top of it that modifies its acoustic quality without changing its basic phonemic identity. Common instances of this additional gesture include lip rounding, in which the lips are rounded at the same time as another constriction is formed elsewhere in the vocal tract, as well as raising the front of the tongue toward the hard palate during the production of a consonant made elsewhere, and raising the back of the tongue toward the velum. Unlike sounds made with lip rounding and tongue-back raising simultaneously, where two constrictions are roughly equal in phonological importance and are usually described as having two co-equal primary places rather than one dominant and one added gesture, a true secondary gesture of this kind is understood as subordinate to a clearly dominant primary articulation. Such secondary gestures are important both for fine-grained phonetic description and for explaining certain phonological patterns, since a sound carrying lip rounding as an added gesture may pattern together with other rounded sounds in assimilation or harmony processes.
Example: The English post-alveolar sounds /ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/, as in 'ship', 'measure', 'chip', and 'judge', involve lip rounding layered on top of their primary place of articulation.

Description: This process is the complete deletion or omission of a sound, typically a vowel or occasionally a consonant, that would otherwise be expected to appear in a word or phrase based on its careful, full pronunciation, often occurring in casual or rapid connected speech as a way of simplifying difficult or awkward sound sequences. It is closely related to but distinct from a process in which a sound becomes weaker or shorter without disappearing entirely, and it is also related to but distinct from a process in which a sound changes to become more like a neighbor rather than vanishing altogether. It commonly targets unstressed vowels in casual speech, especially in fast or informal registers, and it can also affect consonants at word boundaries or within consonant clusters that would otherwise be difficult to articulate smoothly. In many languages, this kind of deletion is a highly productive and pervasive part of everyday spoken style, even though the same words are typically pronounced with the full, unreduced sound sequence in careful, formal speech or in isolated citation form.
Example: In casual speech, 'probably' is often pronounced without its middle vowel as [prɒbli], with the schwa dropped entirely.

Description: This principle in rule-based phonology and morphology states that when two rules could potentially apply to the same input, the more specific rule, defined over a narrower or more particular context, takes precedence and blocks the more general rule from applying in that same context, while the general rule is left to apply everywhere else where the specific rule's conditions are not met. This principle formalizes the intuitive idea that exceptions should override general patterns, and it allows linguists to state a broad, generally applying rule alongside a small number of narrowly targeted special rules without needing to build every exception explicitly into the statement of the general rule itself. This principle is conceptually connected to the notion of a default rule, since the general rule effectively becomes the fallback that covers whatever contexts remain once the specific rule has claimed its narrower territory. This kind of specificity-based rule interaction appears not only in phonology but also in morphology, where more specific morphological rules or irregular forms similarly block more general regular rules from applying to the same lexical item.
Example: The irregular past tense 'went' blocks the general rule adding '-ed', which instead applies to regular verbs like 'walked'.

Description: This process is the addition of an extra sound, usually a vowel or occasionally a consonant, into a word or sequence where that sound was not present underlyingly, most often occurring as a strategy for breaking up a consonant cluster or sequence that would otherwise violate the phonotactic constraints of the language, making the resulting form easier to pronounce or more consistent with the language's preferred syllable structure. The vowel-adding version is especially common when a language strongly disfavors complex consonant clusters or certain coda types, adding a vowel between two consonants that would otherwise be adjacent, while the consonant-adding version typically arises to smooth an awkward transition between two vowels or to strengthen a syllable boundary. This process is one of the core repair strategies available to languages for resolving marked or illegal sound sequences, alongside alternatives such as deletion of one of the offending sounds or resyllabification, and the choice among these strategies can vary both across languages and across different phonological contexts within a single language. In loanword adaptation, this repair is particularly common, since borrowed words often contain consonant clusters that are illegal in the borrowing language and must be repaired to fit its native syllable structure.
Example: Many English speakers add a vowel when pronouncing 'athlete' as [æθəliːt] rather than [æθliːt], breaking up the consonant cluster.

Description: This term names a preference in the rhythmic organization of speech for stressed and unstressed syllables to alternate in a regular, evenly spaced pattern, avoiding sequences in which two stressed syllables occur immediately adjacent to one another, a configuration known as a stress clash, or in which too many unstressed syllables occur in a row without any intervening stress, sometimes called a stress lapse. Languages and speakers often resolve threatened violations of this preference through processes such as stress shift, in which the position of primary stress within a word moves to avoid a clash with a neighboring stressed syllable in connected speech, restoring a more alternating, rhythmically balanced pattern overall. The drive toward this kind of rhythmic balance is understood as a general prosodic tendency rather than an absolute requirement, and it interacts with lexical stress assignment, compound stress rules, and phrase-level intonation to shape the ultimate rhythmic surface form of an utterance. This concept is central to metrical phonology, where rhythmic structure is represented using grids or trees of strong and weak beats, and well-formedness of this rhythmic kind is one of the key criteria used to evaluate whether a given rhythmic structure is optimal.
Example: 'Academic' shifts its stress in 'academic banter' to 'Academic banter' to avoid a stress clash with the following stressed syllable, restoring a balanced alternating rhythm.

Description: This device in metrical phonology sets aside a particular syllable, or sometimes just a final consonant, at the edge of a word, most commonly the final syllable, from the domain over which normal stress-assignment or foot-construction rules operate, effectively making that edge element invisible to the algorithm that builds metrical feet and assigns primary stress. Once the excluded element has been set aside, the regular stress rules of the language apply to the remaining, smaller string of syllables as though that portion were not there at all, and only after stress has been assigned does the excluded syllable get reattached to the word, typically remaining unstressed. This exclusion is often lexically or morphologically conditioned, meaning that only certain classes of words or certain word-final elements, such as a final consonant that does not count toward syllable weight, are treated this way, while other superficially similar words behave according to the regular pattern without any such exclusion. This device allows linguists to maintain simple, general stress rules while still accounting for a systematic class of apparent exceptions concentrated at word edges.
Example: If a language's stress rule normally targets the final syllable but that syllable is set aside from the count, stress instead falls on the second-to-last syllable.

Terminology: feature (binary feature, major class feature, unary feature)
Description: In phonology, this term names one of the small set of primitive articulatory or acoustic properties, such as voicing, nasality, or place of articulation, that are combined together to characterize and distinguish speech sounds, functioning as the basic building blocks out of which contrastive sound units and natural classes are constructed rather than treating each sound as an unanalyzable whole. One type of such a property is specified with one of two opposing values, typically written as plus or minus, indicating whether a sound possesses or lacks it, while another type is either present or simply absent for a given sound, without a contrasting negative value, often used for properties like nasality in frameworks where absence is assumed by default rather than actively marked. A further special subset, covering properties like sonorant and consonantal, together divides all sounds into the broadest fundamental categories, such as vowels, glides, liquids, nasals, and obstruents, before any finer distinctions are considered. This system of properties allows phonologists to state rules and natural classes efficiently by referring to shared values rather than listing individual segments one by one.
Example: The property [+voice] groups /b, d, g, v, z/ together as a natural class distinct from their voiceless counterparts /p, t, k, f, s/.

Description: This term names a table or grid representation that displays, for a set of segments, the specific value of each distinctive property relevant to describing and distinguishing those segments, typically arranged with segments as columns and properties as rows, or vice versa, so that every cell in the table shows whether a given segment is plus, minus, or unspecified for a given property. Such a representation allows linguists to see at a glance exactly which properties differentiate any two segments from each other and to identify natural classes by scanning for groups of segments that share identical values on a particular subset of properties. Because it makes the featural composition of every sound fully explicit, it is useful both for teaching the property system of a language and for formally stating phonological rules, which can refer to entire rows, columns, or sub-blocks rather than listing segments individually. Constructing an accurate version of this representation requires first deciding which properties are contrastive and necessary for the language or sound inventory in question, since including irrelevant or redundant properties can obscure rather than clarify the natural classes it is meant to reveal.
Example: A table for /p, t, k/ would show all three sharing [-voice, -continuant] while differing only in their place values.

Description: One version of this pair of related terms, sometimes distinguished terminologically although the two are frequently used interchangeably in everyday phonetic description, names a consonant produced by a single, very brief and rapid contact of an articulator, typically the tip of the tongue, against another part of the vocal tract, such as the alveolar ridge, with the tongue then moving quickly away again rather than maintaining a sustained closure as in a full stop consonant. The other, naming the associated process, refers to the rule found in many varieties of North American English by which an underlying alveolar stop, particularly /t/ or /d/, is realized this quick, voiced way when it occurs between two vowels and the following vowel is unstressed, producing a rapid, brief burst instead of a fully released stop. Some phoneticians reserve one label specifically for a single rapid contact of the tongue tip against a fixed target and use the other for cases where the tongue tip strikes the roof of the mouth while moving from one position to another, but in the context of English phonology, the process typically refers to this vowel-to-vowel weakening of /t/ and /d/ regardless of the finer articulatory distinction.
Example: In American English, the /t/ in 'butter' is commonly weakened to a rapid tongue-tip contact, giving a pronunciation closer to [ˈbʌɾɚ] rather than a fully released [t].

Description: In metrical phonology, this term names a unit of rhythmic structure consisting of one stressed syllable together with any number of adjacent unstressed syllables that are grouped with it, forming the basic building block from which word-level and phrase-level stress patterns are constructed above the level of the individual syllable. Such units are typically classified according to the position of the stressed syllable within them, with one type having the stress on the first syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables, and another type having the stress on the final syllable preceded by one or more unstressed syllables, and languages differ systematically in which type they favor when building their metrical structure. This theory allows linguists to explain stress assignment not as an arbitrary property attached to individual syllables one at a time, but as the predictable output of a general algorithm that parses a word into such units from one edge and then designates one of them, usually according to its position, as carrying the primary word stress. These units also play a role in explaining rhythmic phenomena above the word level, including the alternation of strong and weak beats in connected speech.
Example: The word 'happy' [ˈhæ.pi] forms a single such rhythmic unit, with stress on the first syllable and the second syllable unstressed.

Description: This term names the concentrated bands of acoustic energy that appear as dark bands on a spectrogram, corresponding to the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract that are amplified as sound produced at the vocal folds passes through and is shaped by the particular configuration of the tongue, lips, and jaw during the production of a vowel or vowel-like sound. Such bands are numbered starting from the lowest frequency, with the first and second being the two most important for distinguishing vowel quality, since the first correlates roughly with vowel height, being higher for low vowels and lower for high vowels, while the second correlates roughly with vowel frontness, being higher for front vowels and lower for back vowels. Because each distinct vocal tract shape produces a characteristic pattern of these resonances, measuring and plotting them is one of the primary quantitative tools phoneticians use to describe and compare vowel systems objectively, rather than relying solely on impressionistic auditory judgments or articulatory descriptions. Such resonances also play an important role beyond vowels, contributing to the acoustic identity of certain consonants such as liquids and nasals.
Example: The vowel /i/ as in 'see' has a characteristically low first resonance and a high second resonance, reflecting its high, front tongue position.

Description: This term describes a situation in which two or more different pronunciations of the same sound or word can occur in the exact same phonetic environment without any change in meaning and without the choice between them being predictable from context, contrasting with a situation where the choice among variants is determined systematically by the surrounding environment. Because the alternation here is not conditioned by any identifiable linguistic factor, the variants are typically considered to be genuinely optional at the level of an individual speaker, arising instead from factors like speech rate, personal habit, social context, or simple random fluctuation rather than from a phonological rule that could predict exactly which variant will occur in a given token. This kind of unpredictable variation is an important concept for defining what counts as an allophone, since variants related this way still do not create a meaning difference even though their occurrence cannot be predicted from environment the way context-conditioned variants can. In practice, apparent cases of this kind sometimes turn out, on closer sociolinguistic or statistical analysis, to be influenced by subtle factors after all, but the label is still used for cases where no clear conditioning environment has been identified.
Example: Some speakers alternate unpredictably between a released and an unreleased final stop in words like 'stop', with either variant possible in the very same context.

Description: This term names a consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract at some point to create a small gap through which the airstream must pass, generating audible, turbulent, hissing or buzzing noise as the air is forced through the constriction, in contrast to stops, which involve a complete closure of the vocal tract rather than a narrow channel. Such sounds can be produced at a wide range of places of articulation, from labial through alveolar, post-alveolar, palatal, velar, and glottal, and at each place they typically come in voiced and voiceless pairs, differing according to whether the vocal folds are vibrating during the production of the noise. Among them, a special subgroup called sibilants is distinguished by a particularly intense, high-frequency, hissing quality, which arises from directing the turbulent airstream against the back of the teeth in addition to the primary constriction, giving them a perceptually much louder and more acoustically salient noise than the non-sibilant members of the category. Sounds of this type are classified phonologically as continuants because the airflow, although obstructed and turbulent, continues throughout the duration of the sound rather than being fully stopped.
Example: /f, v, θ, ð, s, z, ʃ, ʒ, h/ all involve this turbulent, continuous airflow in English, as in 'fan', 'van', 'thin', 'this', 'sun', 'zoo', 'ship', 'measure', and 'hat'.

Description: This acoustic measurement, often abbreviated F0, tracks how many times per second the vocal folds complete a full cycle of vibration during voiced sounds, and it is the primary acoustic correlate of the perceptual quality that listeners experience when they judge a sound as higher or lower, although that perceptual quality is technically the subjective impression rather than the objective physical measurement itself. This measurement is directly determined by properties of the vocal folds, including their length, mass, and the tension applied to them by the laryngeal muscles, with faster vibration producing a higher value and a correspondingly higher perceived quality, and slower vibration producing a lower value and a lower perceived quality. Variation in this measurement over the course of an utterance carries a great deal of linguistic and paralinguistic information, serving as the acoustic basis for lexical tone in tone languages, for word-level tone-accent systems, and for intonation patterns that convey sentence type, focus, and emotional or attitudinal nuance in essentially every spoken language. It is typically measured in hertz and can be visualized as a continuously moving track displayed alongside a spectrogram in acoustic analysis software.
Example: A rising value of this acoustic measurement at the end of an utterance is one common cue that listeners associate with a yes-no question in English.

Description: This theoretical framework, developed primarily within the broader theoretical tradition initiated by Noam Chomsky in the mid-twentieth century, models the sound pattern of a language as a system in which an abstract underlying representation for each morpheme is transformed into its concrete surface pronunciation through the application of an ordered set of formal phonological rules. This approach treats phonological knowledge as part of a speaker's internal, largely unconscious grammar, and it aims to write explicit rules, often stated using distinctive features rather than whole segments, that correctly predict every attested alternation and surface form a native speaker would produce, while also capturing generalizations about which sound patterns are more natural or more common across languages. The classical version of this framework, exemplified by foundational work such as The Sound Pattern of English, places heavy emphasis on rule ordering, since applying the same set of rules in different orders can derive different, sometimes incorrect, surface outputs, making the sequencing of rules a central object of theoretical debate. Later frameworks, including autosegmental phonology, metrical phonology, and Optimality Theory, developed partly as responses to perceived limitations of this earliest rule-based model, though they generally retain its core commitment to explicit, formal, predictive analysis of sound patterns.
Example: An analysis in this tradition proposes an underlying suffix that surfaces as [s], [z], or [ɪz] depending on ordered voicing and epenthesis rules.

Description: This term, also called a semi-vowel, names a sound that is articulated with a vocal tract configuration very similar to that of a vowel, involving a relatively open channel with no significant constriction that would create turbulent noise, but that functions phonologically as a consonant rather than as a vowel, typically occurring in the margins of a syllable, in onset or coda position, rather than serving as the syllable nucleus. Such sounds are characterized by a rapid, transitional movement of the articulators from one position toward a following vowel target, meaning that unlike a full vowel, a sound of this type does not maintain a steady-state articulatory posture but instead is defined mainly by that dynamic movement itself. In English, there are two such sounds, one produced with the front of the tongue raised toward the palate in a position similar to a high front vowel, and one produced with lip rounding and tongue-back raising similar to a high back rounded vowel, and both pattern with consonants for purposes such as article selection and syllabification even though their articulation closely resembles the corresponding vowels. Sounds of this type are grouped together with liquids under the broader category of approximants in many classification systems.
Example: /j/ in 'yes' and /w/ in 'wet' are the two such sounds in English, patterning as consonants despite their vowel-like articulation.

Description: The anatomical space between the two vocal folds within the larynx gives its name to this place of articulation, describing any sound whose primary constriction occurs at this location rather than higher up in the oral or pharyngeal cavity, making the vocal folds themselves the active articulators rather than the tongue, lips, or velum. One specific sound made here is produced by fully closing the vocal folds together, completely blocking the airflow for a brief moment before releasing it, and it functions as a genuine, contrastive consonant phoneme in many languages, while in English it typically occurs as an allophone, most commonly as a realization of /t/ in certain positions, or as an automatic onset marker before vowel-initial words in emphatic speech. More broadly, any secondary involvement of a closure at this location accompanying the production of another sound can range from complete replacement of an oral gesture to a more partial, creaky-voice-like constriction that co-occurs with an oral articulation. Because this location is also the site of voicing itself, sounds made here occupy an unusual position in feature systems, often being treated as unspecified for the features that describe oral place of articulation.
Example: Many English speakers pronounce the medial /t/ in 'button' with a full closure of the vocal folds [ˈbʌʔn̩] rather than as a released alveolar stop.

Description: One member of this pair of syllable weight categories is treated by phonologists as prosodically weighty for purposes of stress assignment and other rhythmic rules, typically because it contains a long vowel, a diphthong, or a closing consonant, giving it greater duration or structural complexity, while the other member lacks these properties, usually consisting of just a short vowel with nothing following it. The precise definition of which category a given syllable falls into varies somewhat from language to language, and this variation is itself an important parameter that phonologists must determine empirically for each language, since some languages count any closing consonant as adding weight while others only count certain types or only distinguish weight based on vowel length. This distinction is central to quantity-sensitive stress systems, in which stress is assigned preferentially to syllables in the weightier category rather than being determined purely by position within the word, and the distinction also plays a role in poetic meter in many literary traditions, where the patterning of the two categories forms the basis of metrical verse structure.
Example: In a quantity-sensitive stress system, a closed syllable like 'CVC' typically counts as belonging to the weightier category, while an open syllable like 'CV' with a short vowel counts as the lighter type.

Description: One term in this contrasting pair describes a relationship between two sounds, most often two consonants, that belong to different, adjacent syllables rather than to the same syllable, meaning that a syllable boundary falls between them, while the other term describes the opposite situation, in which two sounds belong together within a single syllable, with no syllable boundary separating them. This distinction is important for phonological rules that are sensitive to syllable structure, since a rule might apply only to a same-syllable sequence of a nasal followed by a consonant within a single syllable's closing position, but not to a cross-syllable sequence in which the nasal ends one syllable and the following consonant begins the next syllable, even though the two sequences might look identical if syllable boundaries were ignored. Determining which of the two relationships holds for a given consonant sequence often requires independent evidence about syllabification, such as patterns of stress, vowel length, or native speaker intuitions, since the same string of sounds can sometimes be syllabified differently depending on the specific word or the dialect of the speaker. This pair of contrasting relationships is closely related to, and sometimes contrasted with, the concept of ambisyllabicity, in which a single consonant is analyzed as belonging simultaneously to both adjacent syllables.
Example: In 'winter' [ˈwɪn.tər], the /n/ and /t/ typically belong to different syllables, split across the syllable boundary, unlike a cluster contained within a single syllable in a one-syllable word.

Description: This term names a word that is pronounced identically to another word despite differing from it in spelling, meaning, or both, so that the two words share exactly the same sequence of phonemes even though a listener relying only on sound alone would be unable to distinguish between them without additional contextual information. Two words standing in this relationship are described with a related adjective, and this pair of terms is distinguished from words that share identical spelling but may differ in pronunciation and meaning, and from a broader umbrella term that can refer to words sharing either spelling or pronunciation or both. This kind of identical pronunciation arises in a language for a variety of historical reasons, including sound changes that cause originally distinct pronunciations to merge over time, borrowing of words from different sources that happen to converge on the same pronunciation, or simple coincidental similarity, and such pairs are often exploited deliberately for humorous or poetic effect, as in puns, precisely because the identical sound combined with different meaning creates an opportunity for wordplay. This kind of identity can occasionally create genuine ambiguity in spoken communication that must be resolved by context.
Example: 'Bare' and 'bear' share exactly the same pronunciation /bɛr/ in English despite their different spellings and meanings.

Description: This term describes two or more sounds that share the same place of articulation, meaning they are produced with the active and passive articulators positioned at the same location in the vocal tract, even though the sounds may differ in other respects such as manner of articulation or voicing. This label is frequently invoked in phonological analysis to explain why certain consonant sequences are permitted while others are not, since many languages impose restrictions requiring that adjacent consonants, particularly a nasal followed by an obstruent, agree in place of articulation, which is precisely the pattern seen in nasal place assimilation. Recognizing that two segments share their place of articulation this way is also useful for explaining certain historical sound changes and synchronic alternations, since sounds sharing a place are more likely to influence each other through assimilation or to be confused or merged over time than sounds produced at very different locations in the vocal tract. This relational label applies to pairs or sets of sounds rather than describing any single sound in isolation, and it draws directly on the same place-of-articulation categories used elsewhere in phonetic and phonological description.
Example: /m/ and /p/ share their place of articulation, both being bilabial, which is why English words like 'camp' allow this particular nasal-stop sequence.

Description: One member of this pair of metrical units consists of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable, so that the rhythmic pattern rises from weak to strong within the unit, while the other member is the reverse pattern, consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable, falling from strong to weak. In metrical phonology, languages are often characterized as having a general preference for building one or the other type of unit when assigning word stress, and this preference correlates with other systematic properties of the language's rhythm, such as whether stressed syllables tend to be lengthened, in languages favoring the rising type, or whether syllable duration tends to be more uniform, in languages favoring the falling type, a correlation sometimes captured under a broader rhythmic law. These same two labels originate in the study of poetic meter, where a line of verse can be scanned as a sequence of such units, and the terminology was later adapted by linguists to describe the more abstract rhythmic footing that underlies ordinary word stress assignment, independent of any poetic context.
Example: The word 'above' [əˈbʌv] rises from weak to strong within its metrical unit, while 'happy' [ˈhæpi] falls from strong to weak.

Description: This term names the patterned variation in pitch across an utterance that is not used to distinguish the lexical identity of individual words, as lexical tone does in tone languages, but instead operates at the level of the phrase or sentence to convey grammatical, pragmatic, or attitudinal information, such as marking a sentence as a statement versus a question, signaling focus or emphasis on a particular word, indicating that an utterance is complete versus continuing, or conveying emotional nuance like sarcasm, surprise, or uncertainty. This system is typically described in terms of pitch contours or tunes that rise, fall, or combine rise and fall over particular stretches of an utterance, often analyzed using systems that identify discrete high and low pitch targets associated with specific syllables, along with boundary tones that mark the edges of larger prosodic phrases. Although every spoken language uses some version of this pitch-based system to some degree, languages differ considerably in exactly which tunes are available, what meanings they convey, and how tightly the system interacts with syntax and word-level stress or tone. This aspect of prosody is studied both as an autonomous system of meaning in its own right and as one component of the larger prosodic hierarchy that also includes stress and rhythm.
Example: A rising pitch contour at the end of 'You're coming?' signals a question, while a falling contour on 'You're coming.' signals a statement.

Description: This phenomenon is found in many non-rhotic varieties of English in which an /r/ sound is inserted between two vowels across a word or morpheme boundary even though there is no historical or orthographic /r/ present in that position at all, occurring as a way of avoiding an awkward vowel-to-vowel transition, called hiatus, at the boundary between the two words. This process is closely related to a similar phenomenon in which a historically present but otherwise silent word-final /r/ is pronounced specifically because the next word begins with a vowel, and both are commonly explained together as reflecting a more general strategy some non-rhotic dialects use to break up vowel hiatus by inserting a smooth consonantal transition. Because this particular phenomenon inserts a sound that has no historical or spelling justification whatsoever, unlike its silent-r counterpart, it is frequently stigmatized as a pronunciation error by prescriptive commentators, even though it is a systematic, rule-governed, and extremely common feature of many prestigious non-rhotic accents, including many varieties of British English. Its existence is often cited as strong evidence that speakers of these dialects have reanalyzed the historical /r/-insertion rule as a general vowel-hiatus repair strategy rather than as a rule tied specifically to spelling.
Example: Many non-rhotic British speakers insert an /r/ in phrases like 'the idea(r) of it', even though 'idea' has no historical or spelled 'r' at all.

Description: This standardized system of phonetic notation, developed and maintained by the International Phonetic Association, is designed to provide a unique, unambiguous symbol for every distinct speech sound that occurs in any human language, allowing linguists to transcribe the pronunciation of any language consistently regardless of that language's native writing system or spelling conventions. It is built on the principle that each symbol should correspond to one and only one sound and each sound to one and only one symbol, in contrast to ordinary alphabetic spelling systems, which frequently use the same letter for multiple sounds or multiple letters for the same sound, and it supplements its core set of symbols with diacritics that can mark finer phonetic detail such as aspiration, nasalization, length, or secondary articulation. Because it is designed to be universally applicable rather than tied to any single language, it serves as the standard tool used in linguistics, language teaching, speech pathology, and lexicography for representing pronunciation precisely and comparably across languages. Its chart of symbols is organized systematically according to place and manner of articulation for consonants and according to height and backness for vowels, mirroring the underlying articulatory properties the symbols represent.
Example: The English word 'thought' is transcribed using this notation system as /θɔːt/, with dedicated symbols distinct from the ordinary Latin-alphabet spelling.

Description: This process refers to the way the lateral approximant /l/ acquires a secondary articulation involving the raising of the back of the tongue toward the velum, producing a variant commonly called dark 'l', in contrast to the clear 'l' variant, which lacks this raising and has a brighter acoustic quality. In many varieties of English, this process is conditioned by syllable position, typically applying when /l/ is in coda position, either at the end of a syllable or before a following consonant, while the unaffected, clear variant tends to occur in syllable onset position, especially before a vowel. Some varieties of English extend this process much further, applying it to /l/ in essentially all positions, while other varieties, or certain sociolinguistic registers within a variety, show little or no application of it at all, making its degree and distribution a well-studied source of both dialectal and stylistic variation. Because this process changes the acoustic quality of /l/ quite noticeably without changing its phonemic identity, the two resulting variants are treated as allophones of a single underlying lateral phoneme rather than as separate phonemes in the languages where this alternation occurs.
Example: The 'l' in 'milk' typically undergoes this back-of-tongue raising in many English accents, sounding noticeably different from the clear 'l' in 'light'.

Description: This term describes a manner of articulation in which the central part of the tongue makes contact with the roof of the mouth, blocking the direct central airflow path, while the sides of the tongue are lowered or drawn away from the sides of the palate, allowing air to escape freely around one or both sides of the central closure instead. This contrasts with sounds in which airflow passes straight through the middle of the oral cavity rather than being diverted around the sides of the tongue, and this distinction is one of the features used to classify approximants more finely, alongside place and manner. Sounds of this type are cross-linguistically common, appearing at various places of articulation across the world's languages, though English has only a single phoneme of this manner, realized with several different allophonic variants depending on its position in the syllable, most notably the clear versus dark distinction. Some languages additionally contrast a fricative or affricate version of this manner, in which the same side-channel airflow configuration is combined with a narrower constriction that produces audible frication rather than the smooth, vowel-like airflow typical of the approximant version.
Example: /l/ in English, as in 'light' or 'feel', is the only consonant of this manner, with air escaping around the sides of the tongue.

Description: This structure, located in the upper part of the trachea and commonly known as the voice box, houses the vocal folds along with the cartilages and muscles that control their tension, position, and vibration, making it the primary organ responsible for generating voicing and controlling pitch during speech production. Air from the lungs passes upward through it on its way to the pharynx and oral or nasal cavity, and depending on how the vocal folds are positioned, this airflow can be left completely unobstructed, producing voiceless sounds, made to vibrate rapidly, producing voiced sounds, or fully blocked entirely, producing a glottal stop, making this organ the anatomical foundation for the voicing distinction that runs throughout the sound systems of virtually all spoken languages. It is also capable of adjusting the tension of the vocal folds to raise or lower fundamental frequency, giving speakers control over pitch for purposes ranging from lexical tone to sentence-level intonation, and certain languages additionally exploit distinctive settings here such as creaky voice or breathy voice as contrastive or expressive phonation types. Because of its central role, it is often studied together with the broader vocal tract in both phonetics and speech pathology.
Example: Placing two fingers on the front of the neck while alternating between /s/ and /z/ lets you feel the vocal fold vibration controlled by this organ.

Description: One member of this pair of vowel categories is produced with relatively less muscular tension in the tongue and surrounding articulators, typically resulting in a shorter duration and a quality that is often somewhat more centralized, while the other member is produced with comparatively greater articulatory tension, usually resulting in a longer duration and a more peripheral, extreme tongue position closer to the edges of the vowel space. This distinction is used especially to describe pairs of vowels in English that are similar in height and backness but differ systematically along this dimension, and it has consequences for syllable structure, since the less-tense category in many varieties of English is restricted from appearing in open syllables or at the end of a word without a following consonant, unlike the more-tense category, which can occur freely in open syllables. Although the two labels are described impressionistically in terms of muscular effort, they are also correlated with measurable acoustic and articulatory differences, and the distinction functions as a genuine phonological feature in the vowel system of English and several other languages, helping to organize vowel pairs into natural classes for the purposes of phonological rules.
Example: The vowel in 'bit' /ɪ/ belongs to the less-tense category, while the vowel in 'beat' /iː/ belongs to the more-tense category, and unlike /iː/, /ɪ/ cannot end an English word by itself.

Description: This process, common historically and synchronically across many languages, occurs when a consonant becomes weaker or less obstruent, typically shifting along a scale from a stronger articulation toward a phonetically or perceptually softer one, such as a voiceless stop becoming voiced, a stop becoming a fricative or approximant, or a consonant being deleted entirely, usually as the endpoint of progressive weakening. It is frequently triggered by a weak prosodic environment, such as occurring between two vowels, in an unstressed syllable, or at the end of a word, where articulatory effort tends to be reduced compared to strong positions like the beginning of a stressed syllable, and it is understood as the opposite of a process in which a sound becomes stronger rather than weaker. Patterns of this kind are extremely well documented as a diachronic mechanism of historical sound change, famously in the Celtic languages, where the process operates as a productive synchronic morphophonological rule triggered by specific grammatical contexts, but the same general weakening tendency also underlies many everyday allophonic processes in casual speech across unrelated language families, including flapping and spirantization.
Example: The historical shift of intervocalic /p/ to /b/ and eventually to /v/ in many Romance languages is a classic example of this kind of progressive weakening.

Terminology: level of representation (underlying and surface representation)
Description: This term refers to one of the distinct layers of abstraction at which phonologists describe the pronunciation of a word within a rule-based or derivational framework, with one layer capturing the abstract, often invariant form of a morpheme as it is stored in a speaker's mental lexicon before any phonological rules have applied, and another layer capturing the concrete, fully rule-derived pronunciation that is actually spoken and heard. Between these two layers, a derivation may pass through one or more intermediate stages, each reflecting the cumulative effect of applying some subset of the ordered phonological rules, and different theoretical frameworks disagree about exactly how many such layers are necessary and how abstract the earliest one should be allowed to be. Positing a starting layer that is more abstract than any single surface form allows a single stored form to explain multiple related surface alternants through general rules, which is often considered more economical and explanatory than storing every surface variant separately, though this abstractness is also a frequent source of theoretical debate about how psychologically real such abstract starting forms actually are.
Example: An abstract starting form like /rɪd+z/ for 'reads' becomes the concrete, spoken form [rɪdz] after regular voicing agreement rules apply to the plural suffix.

Description: This term names a phonological rule that applies within the word-formation component of the grammar, meaning it operates on individual words or morphemes as they are being assembled, typically before or during word formation and often sensitive to morphological structure, grammatical category, or membership in a specific word class, in contrast to a rule that applies later, after word formation is complete, and typically operates more automatically across larger phrases regardless of morphological structure. Rules of this earlier-applying kind are frequently associated with exceptions, restrictions to particular word classes, and a certain degree of unpredictability or idiosyncrasy, reflecting their close ties to the specific morphological makeup of individual words, whereas rules applying later in the derivation tend to behave more uniformly and exceptionlessly. This distinction in timing of rule application is a central organizing principle of an influential theoretical framework that explicitly divides the grammar into ordered strata, with certain morphological processes and their associated phonological rules applying at earlier strata and others, along with more general phrase-level phonological rules, applying only afterward at a final stage.
Example: A stress-assignment rule that applies only when a specific derivational suffix is attached, and not elsewhere, applies at this earlier, word-formation-sensitive stage.

Description: This phenomenon occurs in non-rhotic varieties of English in which a word-final /r/ that is normally silent when the word appears in isolation or before a consonant is instead pronounced when the following word begins with a vowel sound, effectively joining the two words together with an audible consonant across the boundary between them. This process reflects the historical fact that these dialects lost /r/ only in certain positions, specifically before a consonant or at the absolute end of an utterance, while retaining it in environments where it was followed directly by a vowel, so this phenomenon can be understood as the surviving remnant of the original, fully rhotic pronunciation appearing precisely in the context where historical /r/-deletion never applied. It is closely related to, and often discussed alongside, a phenomenon in which a similar /r/ sound is inserted between vowels even where no historical or orthographic /r/ ever existed, with the two together suggesting that many non-rhotic speakers have generalized a rule requiring an /r/-like consonant before a following vowel across word boundaries, rather than treating this phenomenon merely as an isolated remnant of historical spelling.
Example: In a non-rhotic accent, 'far' is pronounced without /r/ in isolation, but the /r/ is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel, as in 'far away'.

Description: This traditional phonetic and phonological category groups together lateral approximants and rhotic approximants, treating both as sharing enough articulatory and phonological similarities, including their sonorant, vowel-like resonant quality combined with their consonantal syllable-margin distribution, to be classed together under one label despite their quite different individual articulations. Sounds in this category are grouped together with glides under the still broader category of approximants, since neither this category nor glides involve the narrow constriction and resulting turbulent airflow found in true fricatives, but this category is typically distinguished from glides by its somewhat greater degree of vocal tract constriction and by certain characteristic phonological behaviors, such as frequent participation in complex onset clusters together with an obstruent. This category, while useful descriptively and pedagogically, actually covers considerable articulatory diversity across languages, since rhotic sounds in particular can be produced in an unusually wide variety of ways, including as taps, flaps, trills, or approximants at several different places of articulation, meaning that the featural definition of what unifies this whole category cross-linguistically remains a subject of ongoing phonological discussion.
Example: /l/ and /r/ in English, as in 'light' and 'right', both belong to this category, patterning as sonorant consonants distinct from obstruents.

Description: One dimension in this pair of basic descriptive parameters refers to the specific way in which the airstream is modified or obstructed as it passes through the vocal tract during the production of a consonant, encompassing categories such as complete closure followed by release for stops, narrow constriction producing turbulence for fricatives, combined closure and turbulent release for affricates, lowered velum allowing airflow through the nose for nasals, and relatively open, vowel-like configurations for approximants. The other dimension, by contrast, specifies exactly where in the vocal tract this modification of airflow occurs, identifying which active articulator, such as the lips or tongue, approaches or contacts which passive articulator, such as the teeth, the ridge behind them, the palate, the velum, or the glottis. Any given consonant is fully specified only by stating both of these dimensions together, along with its voicing, since one dimension alone identifies a broad category shared by many sounds at different locations, while the other alone identifies a location shared by sounds with different manners, and the standard consonant chart used in phonetics arranges every consonant according to the intersection of these two dimensions.
Example: /t/ and /k/ share one of these two dimensions, both being stops, but differ in the other, alveolar versus velar; /t/ and /s/ share the location dimension but differ in how the airflow is shaped.

Description: This process occurs when the relative order of two sounds within a word is reversed or transposed, so that a sequence that was originally, say, consonant-vowel becomes vowel-consonant, or two consonants swap their positions relative to each other, producing a surface form whose sound sequence differs from the historical or underlying order without any sounds actually being added, deleted, or changed in quality. It can occur as a regular, productive synchronic process in the phonology of a language, systematically reordering sounds in certain predictable environments, or it can occur as a sporadic historical accident affecting only a handful of individual words, sometimes eventually becoming lexicalized as the new standard pronunciation even though it originated as what would once have been considered a speech error or a dialectal variant. It is also well documented as a type of speech error or slip of the tongue in ordinary spontaneous speech production, closely related to but distinct from a spoonerism, since this simpler kind of reordering typically involves swapping sounds within a single word rather than exchanging sounds between two separate words.
Example: The Old English word 'wæps' underwent this kind of sound-order reversal to become modern English 'wasp', swapping the order of the /p/ and /s/ sounds.

Description: This term names a pair of words in a language that differ in meaning and that differ in pronunciation by exactly one sound in exactly the same position, with every other sound in the two words being identical, making pairs of this kind the single most direct and widely used type of evidence for establishing that two sounds are separate, contrastive phonemes rather than allophones of the same phoneme in that language. A weaker but still useful version of the same kind of evidence consists of two words that differ in more than one sound but that nonetheless still support the same phonemic contrast, typically because the additional differences are independently known not to be relevant, allowing linguists to still draw a reasonably confident phonemic conclusion even when a perfect single-sound example cannot be found in the available data. Successfully finding a strict example of this kind for two sounds is considered strong, direct proof that the two sounds must be assigned to separate underlying phonemes, since the meaning difference between the two words can only be attributed to that one sound difference, whereas an inability to find any strict or near example, especially combined with evidence of complementary distribution, instead points toward an allophonic relationship.
Example: 'Pat' /pæt/ and 'bat' /bæt/ differ in meaning by exactly one sound in the same position, showing that /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes in English.

Description: One sound in this family is produced with a complete closure somewhere in the oral cavity, just as with an ordinary oral stop, but with the velum lowered so that air is redirected to flow out through the nose instead of being blocked entirely, giving the sound its characteristic resonant quality despite the oral closure. A vowel can also take on a version of this same quality when it is produced with the velum at least partially lowered during its articulation, allowing some air to escape through the nose simultaneously with the normal oral vowel articulation, which changes its acoustic and perceptual quality compared to a corresponding fully oral vowel with the velum raised and closed. The general process behind this whole family refers to the spreading of this lowered-velum airflow property onto a neighboring sound that would not otherwise have it, most commonly a vowel taking it on because it is adjacent to a consonant of this type, a pattern found across many languages as either an automatic phonetic effect or, in some languages, a fully phonemic and contrastive property of vowels in their own right, independent of any adjacent triggering consonant.
Example: In English, the vowel in 'bang' takes on this lowered-velum quality due to the following consonant, even though the property itself is not contrastive in English vowels.

Description: This term names a set of sounds in a language that share one or more distinctive properties in common and that, as a group, pattern together in the phonological rules of that language, undergoing the same processes or triggering the same effects on neighboring sounds, in a way that would be difficult to state economically if the sounds were simply listed individually without reference to their shared properties. The related concept underlying this notion reflects the idea that phonological rules overwhelmingly tend to target groups of sounds defined by genuine shared properties rather than arbitrary, featurally unrelated groupings, and this tendency is taken as evidence that distinctive properties are not just a convenient descriptive notation but actually correspond to real, cognitively active units that speakers' grammars are sensitive to. Identifying the correct group targeted by a given rule is a central analytical task in phonology, since correctly identifying the relevant shared property or properties allows the rule to be stated in its most general and explanatory form, whereas failing to identify the true group often results in a rule that appears to have unexplained, arbitrary exceptions.
Example: The group of English voiceless obstruents /p, t, k, f, θ, s, ʃ, tʃ, h/ conditions the pronunciation of the plural suffix as [s] rather than [z].
